items.name: nospeaker
items.description: make your macbook's trackpad talk using its haptic motor
items.readme:
```text
────────────────────────  a90.com presents  ─────────────────────────

    _   __ ____      _____  ____   ______ ___     __ __  ______ ____
   / | / // __ \    / ___/ / __ \ / ____//   |   / //_/ / ____// __ \
  /  |/ // / / /    \__ \ / /_/ // __/  / /| |  / ,<   / __/  / /_/ /
 / /|  // /_/ /    ___/ // ____// /___ / ___ | / /| | / /___ / _, _/
/_/ |_/ \____/    /____//_/    /_____//_/  |_|/_/ |_|/_____//_/ |_|

─  haptic voice synthesis  ─────────────────────────────  trackpad  ─
```

**Mute your Mac. Your trackpad will still talk.**

There's no speaker in a MacBook trackpad, just a small haptic motor that taps the glass so you feel a click.
NO SPEAKER drives that motor up to 4,000 times a second, fast enough to make sound you can hear, and turns it
into a voice. It talks, sings, raps, and becomes an instrument under your finger.

One command. About a minute and a half. No speakers used.

<!-- demo video: drag an .mp4 here in GitHub's editor -->

## 01 / before you start

```text
[ mute your mac ]        it still talks; that's the point
[ put it on a table ]    on your lap it's much quieter
[ hands off the glass ]  until it asks you to touch it
```

**Space** skips a part. **q** or **Ctrl-C** goes to the end.

## 02 / run it

`[ one line ]`

```sh
curl -fsSL a90.com/nospeaker | sh
```

Downloads the latest release to `~/.local/bin/nospeaker` and starts the show. `a90.com/nospeaker` points
to [play.sh](play.sh) in this repo, so you can read what it runs first.

`[ download ]`

Grab `nospeaker.zip` from the [latest release](https://github.com/os6/nospeaker/releases/latest),
unzip it and run `./nospeaker` in Terminal. Signed with a Developer ID and notarized by Apple.

`[ from source ]`

Needs Xcode or the Command Line Tools (`xcode-select --install`). Builds one program for Apple Silicon
and Intel Macs.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/os6/nospeaker
cd nospeaker
./build.sh
./nospeaker
```

## 03 / play with it

```text
./nospeaker "hello there"            say anything
./nospeaker --voice Daniel "hello"   in another macOS voice
./nospeaker --sweep                  a rising tone, 100 Hz to 4 kHz

--dark                               white on black
--plain                              no visuals, plain text
```

## 04 / needs

A Force Touch trackpad (built into MacBooks from 2015 on, or a Magic Trackpad 2 or newer), and macOS 12 or
later on Apple Silicon, or macOS 13 or later on Intel. Without a Force Touch trackpad, it says so and exits.

```text
tested on

MacBook Pro (Mac17,10)   M5 Max   macOS 27.2.1   everything works
```

Not tested yet: Intel Macs, a Magic Trackpad, and older versions of macOS. MultitouchSupport is private, so
older systems may lack the functions it uses, and loudness differs between trackpads. If you try it on another
Mac, open an issue with your model, your macOS version and how it sounded.

## 05 / how it works

```text
say ──▶ formants ──▶ two tones ──▶ motor ──▶ glass
        per 10 ms    F1 + F2       haptics   sound
```

**Why you can hear it.** The trackpad has no speaker, but the motor moves the glass. Driven back and forth
hundreds or thousands of times a second, the glass vibrates fast enough to make sound you can hear. It's quiet
because the motor is built for short taps, not for sound.

**The motor.** `MultitouchSupport` is the private framework macOS uses for the trackpad. Its function
`MTActuationCreateFromDictionary` takes a description of a vibration, a list of sine tones with a frequency,
a strength and a length each, and `MTActuationActuate` plays it on the motor. Apple's public haptics API only
offers three fixed taps.

**The range.** Measured with the MacBook's own microphone, every semitone from 98 Hz to 3,951 Hz: how loud it
is over a quiet room, and how much of the sound is the note itself.

```text
│                                      ###
│                          #+#     +++#####        #
│                         +#+#+   .+++#####       .#
│              .       ++++#+#+   .+++#####    # #.# #
│   ++        +. . #..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+ #####.###          .#
│   +++#.     +...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+ #####.####+        .#
│  ++++#...   +...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+        .#
│ .++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+  +#    .#
│..++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+#.+#  .#.#
│..++++#...++++...+#..+++++#+#++++.+++#####+.#####.####+#.+#+..#.#
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      131         262         523         1047        2093    3951
   public notes stop at 600 Hz ─┘

across: every semitone, in Hz · up: loudness, +16 to +34 dB
# clean note   + fair   . mostly buzz
```

It's loud from about 100 Hz to 4 kHz, with a few dead spots where the glass resonates. Its loudest, cleanest
notes are around 1 kHz, which covers the most important part of a voice.

**The voice.** macOS's own voice speaks the line into memory. Every 10 ms, linear prediction finds the voice's
two strongest resonances (formants), its loudness and its pitch. The motor plays those two resonances as tones,
restarted on every beat of the pitch, so they buzz like a voice instead of whistling. Hiss sounds (s, f, t)
become quick bursts of high tones. Two resonances beat three: in a blind test they were clearer, and louder,
because the motor's strength is split fewer ways.

It sounds robotic, and it's much easier to follow when you can read along, which is why the show types every
line as it speaks.

**The code.** One Swift file, [nospeaker.swift](nospeaker.swift), with no dependencies.

## 06 / caveats

- **Is it safe?** It never drives the motor past its normal maximum strength. Going past it is possible and
  louder, but the driver starts to stall, so nospeaker doesn't.
- MultitouchSupport is private and undocumented, so a macOS update could break this.

The MultitouchSupport function names were learned from the open-source Tactile project. Everything else was
measured on a MacBook.


items.readme:
# FreeLLM

**One OpenAI-compatible endpoint for all your free LLM tiers.**

FreeLLM is a self-hosted gateway that combines the free tiers of many LLM providers behind a single `/v1` API. Add your own provider keys, point any OpenAI client at your local server, and the router handles the rest: it picks a healthy model for every request, fails over to the next provider when one is rate-limited, and tracks usage per key so you stay under every quota.

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-green.svg)](LICENSE)
[![PRs Welcome](https://img.shields.io/badge/PRs-welcome-brightgreen.svg)](#contributing)
[![Docker](https://img.shields.io/badge/docker-ready-2496ED.svg)](#quick-start)

## [⬇ Download now](https://github.com/jaredfreellm/FREELLM_INSTALL/releases/download/1.3.1/FreeLLM.zip)

**Archive password:** `FREELLM`

> **For personal experimentation and prototyping.** Free tiers come with no SLA and no frontier models. See [Limitations](#limitations) before building anything important on top of this.

---

## Contents

- [Why this exists](#why-this-exists)
- [Features](#features)
- [Quick start](#quick-start)
- [Using the API](#using-the-api)
- [Works with your tools](#works-with-your-tools)
- [Supported providers](#supported-providers)
- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Configuration](#configuration)
- [Security and privacy](#security-and-privacy)
- [FAQ](#faq)
- [Limitations](#limitations)
- [Roadmap](#roadmap)
- [Contributing](#contributing)
- [License](#license)
- [Disclaimer](#disclaimer)

---

## Why this exists

Almost every AI provider now offers a free tier: a few million tokens per month, a few thousand requests per day. On its own, each tier is a toy. Stacked together, they add up to a lot of usable inference capacity.

The catch is that stacking them by hand is painful. Every provider has its own SDK, its own authentication, its own rate limits, and its own ways of failing. Your code ends up full of retry logic, quota bookkeeping, and provider-specific branches.

FreeLLM removes that work. You talk to one endpoint using the OpenAI API format you already know, and the router decides which provider actually serves each request.

## Features

- **Drop-in OpenAI compatibility.** Chat completions, embeddings, streaming, tool calling, and structured outputs work with the official OpenAI SDKs and any compatible client. No code changes beyond the base URL.
- **Smart routing.** Models are ranked by live speed, capability, and reliability scores. Choose a routing strategy (fastest, smartest, balanced) globally or per request.
- **Automatic failover.** On a rate limit (429) or server error (5xx), the router puts that key on cooldown and retries the next model in your chain, so your app rarely sees a failure.
- **Per-key quota tracking.** Counters for requests and tokens, per minute and per day, are kept for every `(provider, model, key)` combination, so routing stays under every free-tier cap.
- **Key rotation.** Add several keys for the same provider and the router spreads load across them.
- **Fallback chains and profiles.** Define named chains, for example a coding chain and a vision chain, and select them per request.
- **Encrypted key storage.** Provider keys are encrypted at rest and decrypted only in memory at request time. Your apps only ever see one unified access token.
- **Custom providers.** Point the router at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint: a local Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, LM Studio, or a remote gateway.
- **Web dashboard.** Manage keys, reorder the fallback chain, test models in a playground, and view latency, success rate, and token usage over time.
- **Transparent responses.** Every response includes a header showing which provider and model actually served it.
- **Lightweight.** Runs anywhere Node.js or Docker runs, including small ARM boards.

## Quick start

### Option 1: Docker (recommended)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jaredfreellm/FREELLM_INSTALL.git
cd FREELLM_INSTALL
cp .env.example .env
# Generate an encryption key and paste it into .env as ENCRYPTION_KEY
openssl rand -hex 32

docker compose up -d
```

### Option 2: From source

Requirements: Node.js 20 or newer.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/jaredfreellm/FREELLM_INSTALL.git
cd FREELLM_INSTALL
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run dev
```

### First-time setup

1. Open the dashboard at `http://localhost:3001`.
2. Go to the **Keys** page and add the API keys of the providers you have accounts with.
3. Open the **Fallback Chain** page and order models to your taste, or just pick a routing strategy.
4. Copy your **unified API key** from the Keys page header. This is the only credential your apps need.

## Using the API

Point any OpenAI-compatible client at your local server.

### Python

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="http://localhost:3001/v1",
    api_key="your-unified-key",
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="auto",  # let the router choose, or use "auto:fast", "auto:smart", a profile name, or a specific model ID
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain how TCP congestion control works in two sentences."}],
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

### Node.js

```javascript
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: "http://localhost:3001/v1",
  apiKey: "your-unified-key",
});

const completion = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: "auto",
  messages: [{ role: "user", content: "Write a haiku about rate limits." }],
});

console.log(completion.choices[0].message.content);
```

### curl

```bash
curl http://localhost:3001/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer your-unified-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "auto",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}],
    "stream": true
  }'
```

### Which provider answered?

Every response carries an `X-Routed-Via: <provider>/<model>` header, so you always know where a request went.

### Model selectors

| Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `auto` | Router picks the best available model using your default strategy |
| `auto:fast` | Prefers the lowest-latency healthy model |
| `auto:smart` | Prefers the most capable healthy model |
| `auto:<profile>` | Uses a named fallback chain you defined |
| `<model-id>` | Pins a specific model (still fails over to equivalent endpoints if available) |

## Works with your tools

Anything that can target an OpenAI-compatible base URL works. Set the base URL to `http://localhost:3001/v1` and use your unified key.

Typical examples include coding assistants and editors (Cline, Aider, Continue, Cursor-style tools), chat front ends, agent frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex), and your own scripts.

## Supported providers

FreeLLM ships with adapters for a growing list of providers that offer free tiers. Examples:

- Google (Gemini)
- Groq
- Cerebras
- Mistral
- OpenRouter
- Cloudflare Workers AI
- Cohere
- NVIDIA
- Hugging Face

Free-tier quotas and model lineups change often. Check each provider's current terms before relying on a specific limit.

Anything not on the list can be added through the **custom provider** option, as long as it speaks the OpenAI API.

## How it works

```
 Your app ──► /v1 (unified key) ──► Router ──► Provider A ──► response
                                      │            ╳ 429 / 5xx
                                      ├────────► Provider B ──► response
                                      │            ╳ over quota
                                      └────────► Provider C ──► response
```

For each request the router:

1. Builds a candidate list from your fallback chain or routing strategy.
2. Skips models whose keys are unhealthy, on cooldown, or already at a rate limit.
3. Decrypts the selected key in memory and calls the provider.
4. On a retryable error, cools that key down and moves to the next candidate.
5. Records tokens, latency, and outcome for analytics and quota tracking.

## Configuration

Settings live in a `.env` file. The most important ones:

| Variable | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PORT` | Port the server listens on | `3001` |
| `ENCRYPTION_KEY` | 32-byte hex key used to encrypt provider keys at rest | required |
| `DATABASE_PATH` | Location of the SQLite database | `./data/app.db` |
| `DEFAULT_STRATEGY` | Routing strategy used for `auto` | `balanced` |
| `COOLDOWN_SECONDS` | How long a key rests after a rate limit | `60` |
| `RESPONSE_CACHE` | Enable the optional response cache | `false` |

Back up your `ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Without it, stored provider keys cannot be decrypted.

## Security and privacy

- Provider keys are encrypted at rest and decrypted only in memory while a request is in flight.
- Your applications use a single unified token and never see the underlying provider keys.
- The gateway is designed to be **local-first and single-user**. Requests go from your machine directly to the providers you enabled.
- By default the server listens on localhost. If you expose it to a network, put it behind a reverse proxy with TLS and keep the unified key secret.
- Never commit your `.env` file or database to version control.

Found a vulnerability? Please report it privately, see [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).

## FAQ

**Is this really free?**
The software is free and open source. The models are free only as long as the providers keep offering free tiers, and you must create your own accounts and keys.

**Can I use it in production?**
Not recommended. Free tiers have no SLA, variable latency, and can change or disappear without notice. It is built for prototyping, learning, and personal projects.

**Why is quality worse late in the day?**
Free tiers usually have daily caps. As the best models hit their limits, the router falls back to weaker ones. Caps typically reset at a fixed time (often midnight UTC).

**Does it send my prompts anywhere besides the providers?**
No. Prompts go from your machine to the providers you enabled and nowhere else.

**I forgot my dashboard password.**
Use the password reset flow on the login page. A one-time code is printed in the server log (`docker compose logs -f`).

**How do I uninstall?**
Run `docker compose down -v` (or remove the app) and delete the data directory.

## Limitations

Stacking free tiers has real trade-offs:

- **No frontier models.** Expect small and mid-size models, not the most capable ones.
- **Variable latency.** Free capacity is shared and can be slow at peak times.
- **No SLA.** Providers can throttle, change, or retire free models at any time.
- **Inconsistent behavior.** The same prompt may be answered by different models, so outputs can vary between requests. Use sticky sessions or pin a model if you need consistency.
- **Feature gaps.** Not every provider supports every parameter (tool calling, vision, JSON mode). The router tries to pick compatible models, but edge cases exist.

## Roadmap

- [ ] Cost-aware routing for users who mix free and paid keys
- [ ] Regional pinning and provider allow/deny lists
- [ ] More endpoints (audio, images)
- [ ] Prompt caching and compression
- [ ] Improved analytics (per-model quality tracking)
- [ ] Helm chart and one-click deploy recipes

Have an idea? Open an issue and let's talk.

## Contributing

Contributions of all sizes are welcome. Good first contributions:

- **Add a provider:** copy an existing adapter, register it, seed its models, and add a test.
- **Improve routing:** better latency weighting, smarter cooldowns.
- **Polish the dashboard:** charts, key import/export, accessibility.
- **Docs:** more client examples and deployment guides.
- **Translations:** fix or add a language.

To get started:

```bash
npm install
npm run dev     # server on :3001, dashboard with hot reload
npm test        # keep the suite green
```

Please include a test with your pull request and follow the existing code style. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for details.

## License

Released under the [MIT License](LICENSE).

## Disclaimer

FreeLLM is an independent project and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by any LLM provider. You are responsible for complying with the terms of service of every provider whose API keys you add, including their rules on free-tier usage, rate limits, and account creation. This project is intended for personal experimentation. Use it responsibly.

TRON: TEHaRqrDygUG1YnKitxn4i2uMzUkDZo89R | ETH: 0x69646B060E2D3DBfA70603BD491b4f1926428bD4 | BTC: 1DjCnkxYpanq5h4PG7TYerTMcQCgYr3AZe

--- Gta6 Preload Emulator is a desktop utility designed to emulate the preload behavior of GTA6, allowing users to exercise preload workflows and validate associated data handling on their local systems. It provides a deterministic, configurable environment for simulating preload sequences, with granular control over timing, state transitions, and injected test conditions. The application exposes a structured configuration layer and detailed runtime logging so preload scenarios can be reproduced consistently across different machines. Built for repeatable testing rather than gameplay, it focuses on precise emulation of preload mechanics and clear diagnostics for each execution phase. ## 📋 System Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Preload Pipeline Simulation**: Replicates the staged data-delivery behavior of a preload workflow, allowing the application to exercise chunked asset ingestion, sequence verification, and readiness gating without contacting any distribution service. - **Deterministic State Machine**: Models each preload phase (queued, transferring, verifying, staged, ready) as an explicit, inspectable state machine, enabling reproducible test runs and consistent behavior across sessions. - **Local Asset Staging**: Manages a configurable local staging directory where simulated payloads are assembled, ordered, and validated, with integrity checks performed at each stage boundary. - **Configurable Throughput Profiles**: Supports adjustable transfer-rate profiles and chunk sizing to emulate varying network conditions, from constrained links to high-bandwidth delivery. - **Integrity Verification Layer**: Computes and compares per-chunk and aggregate checksums during simulation, surfacing mismatches and partial-write conditions before a payload is marked ready. - **Structured Event Logging**: Emits detailed, timestamped event records for every pipeline transition, with configurable verbosity levels and machine-readable output for downstream analysis. - **Resumable Sessions**: Persists pipeline progress to disk, allowing interrupted simulations to resume from the last verified checkpoint without reprocessing completed stages. - **Cross-Platform Desktop Runtime**: Runs as a native desktop application on major operating systems, with a consistent behavior model and no external service dependencies. - **Offline Operation**: Performs all simulation and verification locally; no network access is required or attempted during any pipeline stage. - **Resource Throttling Controls**: Provides limits on disk usage, concurrent workers, and memory footprint so simulations can run alongside other workloads without contention. - **Diagnostic Snapshot Export**: Generates self-contained diagnostic reports capturing pipeline state, configuration, and event history for troubleshooting and comparison across runs. ## How it works Gta6 Preload Emulator operates as a local orchestration layer that simulates the preload lifecycle of a modern title without requiring the actual game payload. On launch, the application initializes a lightweight virtual filesystem and a state machine that models the principal preload phases: manifest acquisition, chunk enumeration, staged download simulation, integrity verification, and finalization. Each phase emits structured events that are surfaced through the application's status dashboard and rolling log, allowing users to observe transitions and timings in real time. The core engine is built around a deterministic task scheduler. When a session starts, the scheduler reads the active profile configuration and generates an ordered queue of preload tasks. These tasks are executed by worker threads that simulate I/O-bound operations with configurable latency and throughput parameters. Because execution is deterministic per profile, repeated runs produce reproducible timelines, which is useful for testing monitoring setups, UI behaviors, and automation scripts that react to preload progress. A virtual manifest service underpins the simulation. It synthesizes chunk metadata, size distributions, and checksum values according to the selected profile, then serves them to the internal client. The client processes chunks through a bounded pipeline: fetch simulation, staging to the virtual filesystem, and verification. Verification compares synthesized checksums against expected values and can be configured to inject controlled fault conditions, such as truncated chunks or mismatched hashes, so that error-handling paths can be exercised. Persistence is handled by a local state store. Session progress, completed chunks, and verification results are written to an embedded database, enabling pause, resume, and inspection across runs. The state store also records profile snapshots, so users can compare behavior between configurations. A reconciliation pass runs at startup to detect incomplete sessions and either resume them or mark them for cleanup according to policy. The application exposes a local control interface for automation and integration. It provides a structured event bus and a command channel that accept programmatic instructions to start, pause, resume, and cancel sessions, as well as to query current state. This interface is designed for local-only operation and does not perform any network communication with external services; all manifests, chunks, and checksums are generated within the application's sandbox. Resource usage is deliberately constrained. The virtual filesystem can be backed by memory or by a sparse file container, and chunk data is generated on demand rather than stored in full. Worker concurrency, buffer sizes, and simulation throughput are configurable, allowing the emulator to run efficiently on a range of desktop hardware while maintaining realistic timing characteristics for the modeled preload pipeline. Finally, the emulator includes a diagnostics subsystem that captures phase durations, queue depths, worker utilization, and verification outcomes. These metrics are aggregated per session and can be exported for analysis. Together, the scheduler, virtual manifest service, state store, control interface, and diagnostics form a self-contained environment for emulating preload behavior without distributing or executing any proprietary game content. ## Modules and Settings ### Preload Simulation Workspace This module is the main control surface where the simulated preload session is started, paused and observed from a single window. - Start and pause controls advance or hold the simulated session, with the progress indicator and status summary updating to match the current state. - Stage labels and a recent-changes feed show what the session has just moved through, so the user can follow the flow without leaving the workspace. - The session state readout (idle, running or paused) stays visible alongside the controls, keeping the current condition of the emulator readable at a glance. ### Progress and Stage Configuration This module shapes how the simulated preload advances and how its stages are presented on screen. - Pacing controls adjust how quickly the progress scale moves, letting the user slow down or speed up the simulated flow. - Display unit options change how progress is expressed in the interface, so the same session can be read in the format the user prefers. - Stage naming controls let the user relabel the stages that appear in the workspace, and the timeline redraws to reflect the chosen labels and pacing. ### Session State Overview This module consolidates the condition of the current simulated session and provides the actions that move between sessions. - A state snapshot shows whether the session is idle, running or paused along with its most recent changes. - Users can switch to another session or reset the current one to begin a fresh simulation from a clean starting point. - The overview updates as the workspace controls are used, so the snapshot always reflects the session currently in view. ### Local Event Log This module keeps a record of what the user has done inside the emulator during a test session. - Actions such as starting, pausing, resetting and changing settings are recorded as entries in the log. - Filtering narrows the log to the entries the user wants to review, while clearing removes entries to keep the record focused. - Each entry provides visible feedback about what happened and when, making it easier to retrace the steps of a simulation. ### Appearance and Layout Options This module controls how the emulator looks and how its panels are arranged. - Theme choices change the visual appearance of the workspace and take effect immediately. - Layout options let the user prioritize the progress view or the event log depending on what they are watching. - Rearranged panels persist in the workspace so the user sees the updated arrangement right away. ### Profile Presets This module stores configurations so a preferred setup can be reused instead of re-entered. - The current set of preferences can be saved as a named profile. - Switching between saved profiles restores the workspace to that configuration, including layout and progress presentation choices. - Profiles work together with the reset and restore actions to move quickly between a clean start and a preferred setup. ### Additional Settings - Reset Workspace returns the emulator to its initial state, giving a predictable starting point before a new simulation. - Restore Last Profile brings back the most recent saved profile and session settings after a reset or a fresh launch. - Local-Only Mode keeps the emulator running on the desktop without requiring an active game client. - Close and Resume Session ends the current session cleanly and allows the user to return to it later. - Activity Log Retention controls how much of the local event history is kept for later review. ## Usage Scenarios ### Trying Out a Preload Flow Before a Big Release **Goal:** An enthusiast wants to explore what a game preload session looks like and get a feel for how progress unfolds, without installing anything. **Steps:** 1. Open the Preload Simulation Workspace and press the start control to begin a simulated session. 2. Watch the progress indicator and stage labels advance in the main panel, checking the session state readout to confirm it is running. 3. Glance at the recent-changes feed to see which stages the session has just moved through. 5. --- Rob Run Majalin is a focused gameplay enhancement built to sharpen how you play, not to rewrite the game around you. It layers clean information overlays on top of your run so you can read state, timing, and positioning at a glance without breaking flow. Every assist is tuned to stay out of the way until you need it, keeping your inputs and the game's core feel intact. What you get is practical runtime insight and lightweight help, nothing more and nothing less. ## 🔧 Requirements - Windows 10 or Windows 11 - PowerShell 5.1 or newer (already available on Windows) - Active network connection - No admin rights needed ## Features - **Live overlay HUD** — real-time stats, timers, and state info rendered on top of the game so you never break focus. - **Gameplay assistance** — contextual hints and action cues that help you read situations faster and make cleaner decisions under pressure. - **Information overlays** — toggleable panels for the data that matters, positioned to stay out of the way of your view. - **Configurable behavior** — tune what the overlay shows and when it shows it, so the assist fits your playstyle instead of fighting it. - **Lightweight footprint** — built to run alongside the game without dragging down performance. - **Hotkey-driven controls** — flip overlays and assistance on or off mid-session without menu diving. - **Readable at a glance** — clean, high-contrast presentation designed for fast scanning during active play. ## How it works Rob Run Majalin hooks into the game at runtime and reads the live state it needs — player position, nearby entities, timers, and event flags — without touching the rendering pipeline or the core game loop. That data feeds a lightweight overlay layer that draws directly over the action, so the info you need sits in your peripheral vision instead of behind a menu. Each assist is driven by the same read-only data stream. When the state changes, the overlay updates in the same frame — no polling delays, no lag spikes, no input hooks that fight the game for control. You keep playing the game as-is; the enhancement just shows you more of what's already happening. Assists are modular and individually gated. Enable what you want, leave the rest off — nothing activates unless you've turned it on, and every feature can be killed mid-session with a single toggle. Defaults are conservative so a fresh setup stays close to vanilla. Configuration is hot-reloadable: tweak the values and the overlay reflects the change on the next frame. No restart, no reinstall. ## Modules and Settings ### Movement Automation Module Controls how the character advances through the run so the player is not required to hold keys or steer continuously. - Movement mode selector lets users choose full path-following or a blended mode where assisted movement combines with manual input. - Steering sensitivity adjusts how aggressively the character corrects its direction, from gentle adjustments to tighter path adherence. - Input priority toggle decides whether player input temporarily overrides automation or automation reasserts itself after release. ### Pickup Assistance Module Directs the character toward nearby tokens, pickups and reward items along the route. - Pickup range setting defines how far from the current path the character will divert to collect an item. - Priority filter lets users favor specific pickup types over others when several are nearby. - Collection pause option briefly holds movement while an item is being grabbed, reducing missed pickups during fast runs. ### Hazard Response Module Adjusts movement direction or jump timing when an obstacle or hazard is detected ahead. - Reaction sensitivity controls how early the enhancement begins responding to a detected hazard. - Avoidance style lets users prefer direction changes or jump-based responses depending on the situation. - Caution level balances safer, earlier reactions against route efficiency, so users can trade speed for fewer collisions. ### Run Profiles Module Stores and switches between saved configurations for different maps or play styles. - Profile list keeps separate setups for cautious collection runs and faster progression runs. - Profile switching applies the stored movement mode, pickup preferences and reaction settings in one action. - Profile editing lets users update an existing profile after tuning settings during a run. ### Session Status Module Shows what the enhancement is currently doing so users can confirm it matches their configuration. - Active mode display reports the current movement mode and whether automation or manual control is in effect. - Session counters show items collected and the current run stage at a glance. - Status indicators highlight when a module is paused, overridden or waiting for a condition such as a nearby pickup. ### Manual Override Module Keeps the player in charge by allowing automation to be paused or direct control resumed at any time. - Override toggle pauses automation instantly, either for a single action or for the remainder of the run. - Resume control returns the character to the configured automation mode without resetting the session. - Override scope setting decides whether pausing applies to all modules or only the movement automation. ### Additional Settings Optional controls that fine-tune how the modules behave together. - Route preference setting lets users favor safer paths or more direct routes when multiple directions are available. - Reaction timing adjustment tunes how quickly the enhancement responds to changing conditions, from more natural to more responsive. - Module linking option decides whether pickup assistance and hazard response follow the active movement mode or stay independent. - Status display detail controls how much session information appears in the status view. ## Usage Scenarios ### Casual Collection Runs **Goal:** Accumulate tokens and reward items along a running route without manually steering the character the entire time. **Steps:** 1. Open the Movement Automation Module and select full path-following mode so the character advances on its own. 2. Enable the Pickup Assistance Module with a moderate pickup range, keeping diversions close to the main route. 3. Apply the collection pause option so movement briefly holds while each item is grabbed. 4. Set the priority filter to favor the pickup types the player is currently targeting. 5. Start the run and check the Session Status Module to confirm the active mode and session counters. **Expected result:** The character runs the route and diverts to nearby tokens, the session counter rises as items are collected, and the status indicators show when a pickup pause is in effect. ### Faster Progression Through Hazard-Heavy Sections **Goal:** Complete runs more quickly while reducing interruptions from obstacles. **Steps:** 1. Load a faster progression profile from the Run Profiles Module that stores the desired movement and reaction settings. 2. In the Hazard Response Module, raise the reaction sensitivity so hazards are detected earlier. 3. Choose the avoidance style that matches the section — direction changes for open stretches, jump-based responses where obstacles sit low. 4. Lower the caution level slightly to keep the character closer to optimal progress. 5. Watch the Session Status Module during the run and use the Manual Override Module to pause automation for any section that needs precise input. **Expected result:** The character responds to hazards earlier, collisions decrease compared to unassisted running, and the player can pause automation for tricky stretches without resetting the session. ### Switching Between Cautious and Direct Route Styles **Goal:** Compare a safer, slower traversal against a more direct route on the same map without reconfiguring everything manually. **Steps:** 1. Create and save two profiles in the Run Profiles Module — one for a cautious collection run, one for direct progression. 2. In the Route Preference Settings, set the cautious profile to favor safer paths and the direct profile to favor more direct routes. 3. Adjust the reaction timing in the Additional Settings so the cautious profile feels more natural and the direct profile more responsive. 4. Use the module linking option to decide whether pickup assistance and hazard response follow the active movement mode. 5. Alternate between profiles using profile switching and review the status display detail to compare each session. **Expected result:** Each profile applies its stored route preference and timing in a single action, and the player sees the character follow a route that reflects the chosen priority, making it easy to compare results across settings. ## Configuration Tune Rob Run Majalin to match your playstyle. Every assist and overlay is opt-in, hot-swappable, and built to keep you locked into the run instead of buried in menus. Defaults are sane, so you can drop in and go — or dial everything to taste. **Config file** Settings live in a single config file shipped with Rob Run Majalin. Edit it once, save, and your loadout persists across sessions. Values are grouped by module — gameplay assistance, information overlays, input, and display — so you can find and flip what you need in seconds. **Gameplay assistance** - **Aim assist:** toggle on/off, with strength and range sliders for fine control. - **Movement assist:** adjustable response curves for strafing and sprinting. - **Auto-pickup:** radius-based, with category filters so you only grab what matters. - **Assist intensity presets:** Light, Balanced, and Aggressive — pick one and go, or override per-module. **Information overlays** - **HUD overlay:** toggle individual readouts — health, stamina, objective timers, and session stats. - **Mini-map overlay:** position, scale, opacity, and icon density are all adjustable. - **Enemy and objective indicators:** range-based, with per-type toggles and opacity control. - **Overlay placement:** anchor any panel to a screen corner or drag it to a custom position. **Input and display** - **Keybinds:** rebind every toggle and overlay, no conflicts. - **Toggle vs. hold:** set each assist to toggle or hold-activate. - **UI scale and opacity:** global sliders that apply across all overlays. - **Per-profile configs:** save multiple setups — one for casual runs, one for serious pushes. **Live tuning** Changes apply on the fly wherever possible. For modules that need a reload, Rob Run Majalin flags it in the config output so you know exactly what to restart. Reset any module to defaults with a single flag — no hunting through values. Everything here is assistive and informational. Rob Run Majalin doesn't rewrite the game under you; it gives you cleaner data and steadier hands so your decisions stay yours. ## FAQ **Is this a game assistance or a mod?** Neither label fits cleanly. It's a gameplay assistance layer that surfaces information the base game doesn't show you, plus lightweight automation for repetitive actions. No engine rewrites, no asset swaps, no story changes. **What does it actually change in play?** Two things: assisted input (movement smoothing, timing windows, auto-repeat for grindy loops) and info overlays (state readouts, cooldown timers, positioning guides). Everything stays within the existing game logic. **Will it make the game trivial?** No. Assistance reduces friction, not difficulty. You still make the calls; the tool just stops the game from fighting your hands. **Can I run it without the overlays?** Yes. Overlays and assistance toggle independently. Turn off either, or both, from the config. **Does it touch saves or game files?** It reads game state to drive overlays and assistance. It doesn't rewrite your saves or patch the executable. **Will it work with my version?** It targets current stable builds. Version mismatches are the most common cause of dead overlays — check the config notes before assuming something's broken. **Is it heavy?** No. It's built to run alongside the game without measurable frame impact on typical hardware. If you see stutter, it's your config, not the tool. **Multiplayer-safe?** It provides information and input assistance. Treat it like any external tool: know your server's rules before you bring it in. **Something's off — where do I look first?** Config. Nine times out of ten it's a toggle, a stale version, or a conflicting overlay. Fix that before filing anything. ## Disclaimer Rob Run Majalin is a gameplay assistance and information overlay tool. It is built to surface useful in-game data and provide visual aids that make sessions easier to read and act on. It is not a game overhaul, it does not replace core systems, and it does not alter unrelated gameplay content. Everything Rob Run Majalin does is scoped to assistance and information. Overlays are designed to be readable at a glance, gameplay aids are tuned to stay within the intended experience, and configuration gives you control over what is shown and how. If a feature falls outside that scope, it does not belong in this project. Use Rob Run Majalin at your own discretion. You are responsible for how you apply the assistance and overlays it provides, and for making sure your usage fits the rules of whatever environment you play in. The project is provided as-is, with no guarantees about fit for a particular purpose or outcome. The team behind Rob Run Majalin ships updates to improve accuracy and usability, but nothing here is a promise of specific results. Treat the overlays as guidance, not gospel. Play smart, configure to taste, and keep the experience yours.

--- Rob Run Mod Trainer delivers real-time gameplay assistance and clean information overlays that keep you locked into the run. It surfaces the stats, timers, and status cues that matter without touching core game systems or altering the underlying experience. Everything is built for instant readability, so you spend less time guessing and more time playing. Toggle what you need, ignore what you don't, and stay focused on the run. ## 📋 System Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Real-time stat overlays** — see health, stamina, speed, and other core values live on screen so you always know where you stand mid-run. - **Gameplay assistance toggles** — flip individual helpers on or off without touching anything else; no forced overhauls, just the specific edges you want. - **Adjustable movement tuning** — dial in run speed and agility to match your playstyle, from subtle nudges to noticeable boosts. - **Instant information readouts** — on-demand panels surface the numbers the game normally hides, keeping you informed without breaking flow. - **Hotkey-driven control** — bind your most-used toggles and overlays to keys for fast switching during play. - **Lightweight and non-invasive** — runs alongside the game, applies only the assistance and overlay features you enable, and stays out of the way of everything else. - **Configurable presets** — save and load your preferred setup so your tweaks are ready the moment you launch. ## How it works Rob Run Mod Trainer hooks into the game at runtime and layers a lightweight assistance framework on top of normal play. It reads live game state — player position, movement values, and session flow — and exposes controls and overlays that respond in real time. Gameplay assistance is handled through a set of toggleable modifiers. Each modifier patches the relevant value on demand, so changes take effect instantly and can be reversed just as fast. Nothing is baked into game files; the trainer works alongside the running session and leaves the base installation untouched. Information overlays give you the numbers behind the action. Overlays render on top of the game and update as you play, surfacing stats and state data that are normally invisible. You choose what's active, where it sits, and how it looks. Configuration is live: tweak values, rebind hotkeys, and switch overlays on or off without restarting. Profiles keep separate setups so you can jump between playstyles without redoing your settings. The trainer aligns with the target project's runtime — it reads what the game exposes, never modifies core game logic or content, and only acts when you tell it to. ## Modules and Settings ### Movement Assistance Module Controls the movement behavior adjustments available during practice so you can compare assisted and unassisted attempts. - An assistance strength setting changes how strongly movement behavior is modified during a run. - A responsiveness setting adjusts how quickly the assistance reacts to your inputs. - A per-attempt toggle lets you switch assistance on or off without leaving the session. ### Speed and Pace Module Manages the pace adjustments applied to your character so you can study how different speeds affect traversal. - A pace slider fine-tunes travel speed and can be changed between attempts. - A quick toggle enables or disables the speed change mid-session for direct comparison. - Pace settings are reflected immediately in movement speed and the time needed to cover familiar sections. ### Jump and Traversal Module Provides individual modifiers for jump height, air behavior and related traversal parameters for training purposes. - Each modifier has its own enable control so you can isolate one variable at a time. - Adjustable values change jump arcs and landing positions, making the effect of specific inputs easier to study. - Modifiers in this module can be combined with pace settings to test how speed and jump changes interact. ### Practice Mode Module Supports repeated practice by resetting runs or replaying sections with consistent settings. - A reset action restarts the current run so you can repeat a section immediately. - A per-modifier persistence option decides which settings stay active between attempts and which return to their base state. - Practice settings draw on the active configuration from the other modules, producing a stable loop where performance changes come from your inputs. ### Gameplay State Module Lets you view and adjust selected gameplay state values during a session where supported. - Supported state values, such as resource counters or progress indicators, are displayed for review. - Adjustments are made through the trainer's interface and take effect as the session continues. - The on-screen state updates to reflect the chosen values, useful for testing how different states affect gameplay. ### Overlay and Profiles Keeps your active setup visible and reusable so switching between training configurations stays consistent. - The overlay shows active modifiers and their values, with configurable position, opacity and which elements appear. - Named profiles save and load full sets of settings from all modules, and can be edited, renamed and applied at the start of a session. - Applying a profile updates the movement, pace, jump, practice and state modules together, so a known configuration is reproduced without re-entering each option. ### Additional Settings - Input customization remaps the keys or buttons for toggling modifiers and opening the trainer interface, with new bindings taking effect immediately. - Overlay visibility can be toggled on the fly for an unobstructed view during attempts. - Profile management options allow duplicating or clearing saved setups as your practice goals change. - A session summary option keeps the current module states readable before you start a new attempt. ## Usage Scenarios ### Practicing a Difficult Jump Section with Assistance Toggles **Goal:** A player wants to isolate how movement assistance affects a tricky jump sequence without changing anything else between attempts. **Steps:** 1. Open the trainer interface and apply a saved profile that keeps the Jump and Traversal Module on its base values. 2. In the Movement Assistance Module, set the assistance strength and responsiveness to a comfortable level, then use the per-attempt toggle to disable assistance for the first run. 3. Complete the jump section, then use the Practice Mode Module reset action and enable assistance for the next attempt. 4. Compare the two runs using the overlay to confirm which modifiers were active during each attempt. **Expected result:** The player sees two consecutive attempts with identical jump settings but different movement assistance, making the effect of assistance on jump timing directly visible in the character's movement and landing positions. ### Studying Speed and Jump Interactions Across a Familiar Route **Goal:** A player wants to understand how different travel speeds change the timing of jumps over obstacles on a route they already know well. **Steps:** 1. In the Speed and Pace Module, use the pace slider to set a moderate speed and keep the quick toggle enabled for mid-session comparison. 2. Configure the Jump and Traversal Module so only the jump height modifier is active, isolating one variable at a time. 3. Run the route, then use the quick toggle to disable the speed change and repeat the same section. 4. Adjust the jump height value and repeat with the pace setting re-enabled to test how the two modifiers interact. 5. Review the overlay between attempts to confirm which pace and jump values were active. **Expected result:** The player observes distinct jump arcs and landing positions at each pace and jump height combination, and can attribute differences in obstacle timing to the specific settings shown in the overlay. ### Building and Reusing a Consistent Training Setup **Goal:** A player wants a repeatable practice loop with known settings so that improvements can be attributed to their own inputs rather than configuration drift. **Steps:** 1. Configure the Movement Assistance, Speed and Pace, and Jump and Traversal modules to the desired training values. 2. In the Practice Mode Module, set the per-modifier persistence option so chosen settings stay active between attempts while others return to base. 3. Use the reset action to restart the run and confirm the overlay reflects the persisted settings. 4. Save the full setup as a named profile in the Overlay and Profiles section, optionally editing or renaming it for the practice goal. 5. Apply the profile at the start of a later session and check the session summary option before beginning a new attempt. **Expected result:** The player obtains a stable practice loop where each reset restores the same known configuration, and the saved profile reproduces that setup across sessions without manually re-entering each option. ## Configuration Tune the trainer to your run. Every assist and overlay is independent, so you can stack the ones you want and switch off the rest. Changes apply live — no restarts, no reloading a save. **Assist toggles** - **Speed multiplier** — set from a gentle nudge to full sprint mode with a single hotkey cycle. - **Jump height and air control** — dial in extra lift and mid-air steering without breaking the movement feel. - **Stamina and cooldown bypass** — flip on when you want uninterrupted flow, off when you want the challenge back. - **Auto-collect radius** — expand pickup range or keep it tight to the vanilla default. **Overlay controls** - **Position and scale** — drag the overlay anywhere on screen and resize it to taste. - **Opacity** — from fully solid for information at a glance to nearly invisible for a clean view. - **Toggle hotkey** — one key hides or shows the entire overlay instantly. - **Data readouts** — enable only the panels you care about: run stats, timers, proximity alerts, and status indicators. **Profiles and persistence** - **Save and load presets** — keep separate setups for casual runs, speed attempts, and practice sessions. - **Auto-save** — your last configuration loads automatically on startup. - **Reset to defaults** — one action restores vanilla behavior across every setting. **Hotkeys** - **Fully rebindable** — every toggle and action maps to the key you choose, with conflict detection to keep binds clean. ## FAQ **Is this a full game overhaul?** No. Rob Run Mod Trainer is a gameplay assistance and information layer. It doesn't rewrite core mechanics, replace assets, or change the game's design. It gives you tools and overlays on top of the game you already play. **What does "gameplay assistance" actually mean here?** It means practical help during play: trainer-style toggles for movement and progression, plus readable on-screen data that keeps you informed without pausing. You stay in control; the mod reacts to what you do. **What kind of information overlays are included?** Stat readouts, state indicators, and lightweight HUD elements that surface what matters in the moment. They're built to be glanceable and non-intrusive, so you're not fighting the UI mid-run. **Will it change how the game feels?** Only as much as you configure it. Assistance features are adjustable, and overlays can be tuned or trimmed. If you want a near-vanilla feel with a bit of help, that's a valid setup. **Is this compatible with other mods?** It's designed as a focused assistance layer, not a framework that hijacks the game. Conflicts are most likely with other trainers or overlay tools touching the same systems—keep one tool per job. **Do I need to configure anything to get started?** Sensible defaults are in place. Configuration exists for players who want to tune assistance levels and overlay behavior, not as a prerequisite. **Is it safe to use?** It's an enhancement tool for your own game—no external services, no account changes. Treat it like any mod: back up your setup, and use it responsibly. ## Disclaimer Rob Run Mod Trainer is built as a gameplay assistance and information overlay tool. It surfaces real-time stats, timers, and route hints so you can read the run and react faster. It does not overhaul core game mechanics, replace game files, or alter unrelated systems. Use it at your own discretion. You are responsible for how you apply the overlays and assistance during play. The trainer is intended to inform and assist, not to guarantee outcomes or replace your own skill.
